explained.headline: Brazil votes in presidential runoff between Lula and Bolsonaro

happened.text: In the first round of voting earlier in the month, Flavio Bolsonaro surpassed Lula by more than 2.2 million votes.
Preliminary election results are expected on Sunday night.

background.text: Flavio Bolsonaro is a 45-year-old senator who has sat in the Senate since 2019 and is the eldest son of former president Jair Bolsonaro.
Jair Bolsonaro is currently under house arrest serving a sentence for attempting a coup to overturn his 2022 election defeat.

matters.text: Sources note that the election will determine Brazil's future political direction and its relationship with the United States.
DW reports that if Flavio Bolsonaro wins, it could determine the extent to which the United States expands its influence in Latin America.
The Guardian reports that analysts believe Flavio Bolsonaro could refuse to concede if Lula wins, and that Donald Trump might refuse to recognise the result.

uncertain.text: Recent polls have shown the candidates virtually tied, leaving the outcome of the runoff highly unpredictable.
It remains uncertain how many voters who identify with neither candidate will turn out or how the large pool of uncommitted voters will break.

terms.definition: A secondary voting contest held between the top candidates when no contender secures an absolute majority in the initial round.

removed.text: Brazilians are heading to the polls on Sunday for a presidential runoff election between the incumbent leftist Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva and the right-wing senator Flavio Bolsonaro.
why: The evidence identifies Flavio Bolsonaro as the son of Jair Bolsonaro, not the incumbent.

removed.text: Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva is an 80-year-old veteran politician who previously served as head of state from 2003 to 2010 and took office again in 2023.
why: Evidence states Lula is 80, but does not confirm he took office in 2023.

explained.headline: Ukraine reports restored Starlink speeds amid dispute over restrictions

happened.text: Ukrainian officials announced that the connection speeds for the Starlink satellite internet system and its military counterpart Starshield have returned to normal after more than a week of restrictions.
Elon Musk stated that his company SpaceX restricted Ukraine's Starlink internet service because the military violated terms of service by using it for offensive drone strikes.

Serhii Beskrestnov, a Ukrainian presidential adviser, stated that Starlink terminals operating in Ukraine have a speed restriction and do not work on Russian territory, making deep strikes physically impossible.

background.text: Elon Musk is a tech billionaire who owns SpaceX, the aerospace company that provides the Starlink satellite internet network.
Donald Trump is the President of the United States, whose administration experienced a diplomatic standoff with Kyiv regarding Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil infrastructure.

matters.text: Ukrainian officials stated that the speed restrictions hampered the military's ability to intercept Russian attack drones and forced the cancellation of combat missions.
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned that the connection limits would cause significant human losses.
Elon Musk asserted that if Starlink were to be switched off entirely, the Ukrainian front line would immediately collapse.

uncertain.text: It remains unclear who was ultimately responsible for the Starlink slowdown that occurred.
Kyiv has questioned Washington's support over intelligence sharing amid speculation that the White House may have ordered restrictions on the Starshield system.

terms.definition: A satellite internet constellation operated by aerospace company SpaceX.

removed.text: Volodymyr Zelensky is the president of Ukraine, which relies heavily on Starlink terminals for military coordination and communications on the battlefield.
why: Evidence confirms the importance of Starlink to Ukraine, but doesn't explicitly state Zelensky is currently president.

background.text: Gadi Eisenkot is a former army chief who leads the liberal Yashar party.
Israel's proportional representation system requires parties to form coalitions to secure a governing majority because no single party has ever won an outright majority.

explained.headline: Nearly 1,000 arrests made as protests and clashes sweep France

happened.text: While demonstrations were largely peaceful, police fired tear gas and water cannon in several cities, and some protesters set barricades on fire or smashed shop windows.
French interior minister Laurent Nuñez stated that two people were seriously injured during the unrest.

background.text: The unrest follows weeks of high school demonstrations that began in mid-September over staff shortages, crumbling buildings and overcrowded classrooms, which later drew in trade unions, teachers and parents.
Mass demonstrations also took place in other European cities, including Barcelona, Tirana, Brussels and Milan.

matters.text: Radical left presidential candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon stated that Emmanuel Macron must give in and address social grievances or else face repeated protests every week.
Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez stated that the nationwide number of arrests would likely rise as the situation develops.
The ongoing protests set the stage for a highly divisive presidential election period with voters facing choices between opposing political forces.

uncertain.text: Official estimates and union figures regarding the turnout differed significantly, with the interior ministry estimating 410,000 protesters and unions putting the figure at about 800,000.
It remains to be seen whether the government and protesters will find a political resolution to satisfy the demands of students and trade unions.

removed.text: Nearly 1,000 arrests were made across France as hundreds of thousands of people took part in demonstrations over the cost of living and poor school conditions.
why: The evidence does not explicitly link the cost of living and schools to this specific protest day.

removed.text: Emmanuel Macron serves as the French President, and he faces a political crisis as he prepares to leave office next spring.
why: Evidence does not mention he is leaving office next spring.
